newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Meridor says deeper cuts may be needed.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Meridor says deeper cuts may be needed.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor said on Tuesday that further spending cuts may be necessary in 1997 in light of lower-than-forecast revenue.

"If it becomes clear towards the end of the year that we will not achieve the revenue level that is required for financing expenditures, we will deal with it at the beginning of the year and again by cutting spending but it is still too early to know at this stage," Meridor told the parliamentary finance committee.

The government has approved cutting 4.9 billion shekels or 3.2 percent of spending in 1997. The Finance Ministry at the end of the month will submit this budget to parliament, which has until the end of the year to approve it.
The widening government budget deficit has worried the government, which had set a deficit target of 7.6 billion shekels for 1996.
Forecasts now call for this deficit target to be surpassed by about four billion shekels and officials have blamed lower-than-expected revenues since the beginning of the year.
Separately, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Meridor, Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel and business leaders met on Tuesday afternoon to discuss the situation of the economy.

While no decisions were taken the industrialists argued for the need of an economic package that would include a currency devaluation to boost exports and a reduction in labour costs, sources at the meeting said.
The economic leaders decided to continue the discussion at another meeting but no date was set.
At the meeting Netanyahu expressed concern over the situation of exports, which have been hurt by a strong shekel.
